passages.t: The garden, and the wedding fulfilled
passages.happening:
The man answers the bride's invitation. ‘I have come to my garden, my sister, my bride; I have gathered my myrrh with my spice’ (verse 1). He has eaten honey and drunk wine and milk.

Then a voice speaks to the lovers: ‘Eat, O friends, and drink; drink freely, O beloved’ (verse 1).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 4 ended with her invitation for her beloved to come into his garden. This verse answers it, and the wedding section (3:6 to 5:1) reaches its fulfillment and close. It is told entirely in pictures of a garden, spices, honey and wine.

The last line is spoken by an unnamed voice, perhaps the wedding guests, perhaps the poet. Some ancient readers heard God himself welcoming the union. Either way, the love of husband and wife is welcomed, not hidden in shame.
passages.later: The Bible's first marriage is greeted the same way: ‘For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh’ (Genesis 2:24).
passages.asks: The voice tells the lovers to eat and drink freely. If you are married, ask what it would mean to receive married love as a gift to enjoy, not a duty or a shame. And ask how a wedding you have seen showed you something of God's goodness.

passages.t: A knock at night, and the watchmen
passages.happening:
‘I sleep, but my heart is awake’ (verse 2). Her beloved knocks and asks her to open, his hair wet with the dew of the night. She hesitates: she has taken off her robe and washed her feet, must she get up again? (verse 3).

He puts his hand to the latch, and her heart pounds for him (verse 4). She rises to open, her hands fragrant with myrrh on the bolt (verse 5). ‘I opened for my beloved, but he had turned and gone. My heart sank at his departure. I sought him, but did not find him. I called, but he did not answer’ (verse 6).

Then: ‘I encountered the watchmen on their rounds of the city. They beat me and bruised me; they took away my cloak, those guardians of the walls’ (verse 7).

Even so, her words to the daughters of Jerusalem are not bitter: ‘O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you, if you find my beloved, tell him I am sick with love’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
After the height of union comes a scene of hesitation, loss and pain. This is the second night search in the book (compare 3:1-5), and it is harder: the watchmen are violent, and he is not found at once.

Doors were usually fastened by a wooden bolt on the inside, which could be moved from outside by reaching through a hole. People went barefoot or in sandals, and washing the feet was part of going to bed. Her excuses are the kind anyone might make when woken.

The scene begins with a dreamlike line, ‘I sleep, but my heart is awake’ (verse 2), and it is told in quick, vivid steps. It is told in images, not description.

A woman alone in the streets at night was in danger. Taking her cloak may have been meant to shame her as well as hurt her.
passages.later: The psalms speak for those who are beaten and wronged: ‘The LORD is a refuge for the oppressed, a stronghold in times of trouble’ (Psalm 9:9). And they charge those with power to protect, not harm: ‘Defend the cause of the weak and fatherless; uphold the rights of the afflicted and oppressed’ (Psalm 82:3).
passages.hard:
Why is the woman beaten by the watchmen, and what does the scene mean?

The scene is troubling, and interpreters read it in different ways.

Many take verses 2 to 8 as a dream, since the scene begins with her saying she is asleep but her heart is awake, and dreams can move suddenly from longing to fear. On this reading the beating expresses the anxiety and pain of separation, not a literal event.

Others read it as a real event. A woman alone in the streets at night was in danger in the ancient world. The watchmen may have taken her for a woman of the street, and their violence is an injustice that the text records without approving.

Older allegorical readers took the watchmen as religious leaders, or as trials that wound the soul seeking God.

The Song does not explain the scene or say what happened to the watchmen. It shows that love's search can be costly, and it shows her love surviving the cost. Her next words are not bitterness but a charge to tell her beloved that she is sick with love.

On every reading, the scene gives no warrant for violence against anyone. Those who were meant to guard her harmed her, and the Song does not call that right.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: She hesitated, and when she opened, he was gone. Ask whether there is someone you have kept waiting at the door, and what it would mean to open now. And if you have been hurt by those who should have protected you, ask whom you could trust to tell.

passages.happening:
The daughters of Jerusalem ask, ‘How is your beloved better than others, O most beautiful among women?’ (verse 9).

She answers with a poem of praise. ‘My beloved is dazzling and ruddy, outstanding among ten thousand’ (verse 10). ‘His head is purest gold; his hair is wavy and black as a raven’ (verse 11). His eyes are like doves by streams of water (verse 12). His cheeks are like beds of spice (verse 13). His arms are gold set with jewels, and his legs pillars of marble (verses 14-15). ‘His appearance is like Lebanon, as majestic as the cedars’ (verse 15).

‘His mouth is most sweet; he is altogether lovely. This is my beloved, and this is my friend, O daughters of Jerusalem’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This is the only poem in the Song that praises the man part by part. It uses pictures of precious metals, stones and ivory, and many readers notice that it describes him almost like a statue, a figure of great worth. Ivory work was prized in ancient Israel, and carved ivory panels from the ninth or eighth century BC have been found at Samaria. Lebanon's cedars stood for majesty and strength.

The poem moves from his head down to his legs and ends with a summary: he is her beloved, and her friend. Love and friendship are held together.

Her love has not shrunk because he was gone. If anything, his absence has made her praise him more.
passages.later: The cedars of Lebanon were the Bible's picture of strength: ‘The righteous will flourish like a palm tree, and grow like a cedar in Lebanon’ (Psalm 92:12). And Amos knew the ivory of Samaria's rich houses: ‘the houses of ivory will also perish’ (Amos 3:15).
passages.asks: She calls him her beloved and her friend. If you are married, ask whether your husband or wife is also your friend, and what would deepen that friendship. And ask whom you could praise this week as warmly as she praises him.
